question.text:
A 25-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 39 weeks of gestation presents to the obstetrics unit of the hospital for planned C-section. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, and she takes a prenatal vitamin every day. She has had no recent illnesses or sick contacts. Temperature is 37.0 ºC (98.6 ºF), pulse is 96/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and blood pressure is 108/60 mmHg. On physical exam, the patient is well-appearing with a gravid abdomen. Fetal heart tracings are reassuring. She is not currently in labor and amniotic membranes are intact. The patient’s urine culture was negative at the initial prenatal appointment but vaginal-rectal culture at 37 weeks was positive for group B *streptococcus* (GBS). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
Answer Choices: (A) Cefazolin for GBS prophylaxis due to planned C-section (B) Observation without antibiotic intervention (C) Urine culture (D) Vaginal-rectal culture (E) Postoperative antibiotics for GBS prophylaxis (F) Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis (G) Standard preoperative antibiotics plus group B streptococcal treatment (H) Repeat vaginal-rectal culture at delivery (I) Standard preoperative antibiotics (J) No intrapartum antibiotics

options.A: Cefazolin for GBS prophylaxis due to planned C-section
options.G: Standard preoperative antibiotics plus group B streptococcal treatment

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is at 39 weeks gestation with a positive GBS vaginal-rectal culture. The standard of care for GBS-positive mothers at term is intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis to prevent neonatal GBS infection. C-section is planned, so the antibiotics should be administered before the procedure.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Positive GBS vaginal-rectal culture at 37 weeks gestation.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While a urine culture is important for other infections, it is not the primary concern in this case. Observation without antibiotics is not appropriate given the positive GBS culture. Postoperative antibiotics are not the primary intervention for GBS prophylaxis. A repeat vaginal-rectal culture at delivery is unnecessary and delays appropriate treatment. Standard preoperative antibiotics are not the most appropriate choice as the patient is already at term and has a positive culture. No intrapartum antibiotics is not appropriate given the positive GBS culture.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is at 39 weeks gestation with a positive vaginal-rectal GBS culture, indicating colonization. Since she is having a planned C-section, intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis (F) is the most appropriate measure to prevent GBS transmission to the newborn during the surgical procedure. This is a standard protocol for women with GBS colonization at term, regardless of culture site, when delivery is anticipated.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Positive vaginal-rectal culture for GBS at 37 weeks
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Other options like postoperative antibiotics (E) or standard preoperative antibiotics (I) are less specific to the intrapartum risk. Observation without intervention (B) is not appropriate given the known colonization. Repeating culture at delivery (H) is unnecessary since the risk is already established. Prophylaxis during labor (F) is the most targeted and effective approach for a planned C-section.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is at 39 weeks gestation with a planned C-section and has a positive vaginal-rectal culture for GBS at 37 weeks. According to current guidelines, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with penicillin is recommended for all women who test positive for GBS at any time during pregnancy, regardless of labor status, to prevent neonatal GBS infection. Cefazolin is not the first-line agent for GBS prophylaxis in obstetrics.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Positive vaginal-rectal culture for GBS at 37 weeks, with planned C-section at 39 weeks.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other options like observation (B) or repeat culture (H) are inappropriate because GBS colonization mandates prophylaxis. Urine culture (C) and vaginal-rectal culture (D) are not needed as the latter is already positive. Postoperative antibiotics (E) are not standard for GBS prophylaxis in C-sections; intrapartum prophylaxis is preferred. Cefazolin (A) is not first-line for GBS in obstetrics.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: A and G consider timing of antibiotics, but GBS prophylaxis is administered before delivery, not preoperative/postoperative. B, C, E, H, I, and J are either too late, not evidence-based, or not indicated in this scenario.
